What Is AI Literacy, and What Does the EU AI Act Require?

Explainerlowob research

By lowob · 17 November 2026 · 5-minute read · Strategy

In short: AI literacy is the skills, knowledge and understanding that let people use AI systems in an informed way and see their opportunities, risks and possible harms. Article 4 of the EU AI Act requires providers and deployers to take measures that support AI literacy among their staff and others using AI on their behalf. Since the Digital Omnibus amendment took effect on 27 July 2026, the duty is one of effort: no specific level has to be guaranteed for any individual.

Key points

  • The original Article 4 required measures to ensure, "to their best extent", a sufficient level of AI literacy; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 replaced this with measures "to support the development of AI literacy".
  • The amended text states the duty "does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual".
  • The Commission's Q&A, updated 20 October 2026, says no certificate is needed and that national supervision and enforcement apply from 2 August 2026.
  • Deployers of high-risk systems have a separate duty under Article 26(2) to assign human oversight to people with the necessary competence, training and authority.

What AI literacy means

Article 3(56) defines AI literacy as the skills, knowledge and understanding that allow providers, deployers and affected persons to make an informed deployment of AI systems and to gain awareness of their opportunities, risks and possible harm.

In a company, that means role-specific knowledge. A seller using a drafting assistant needs to know it can invent facts and what data must never go into it. An owner of a hiring tool needs far more. Literacy is about limits and judgment, not prompting tips or a general course on neural networks.

What Article 4 required, and what changed in 2026

The duty has applied since 2 February 2025. The 2026 change is to its strength, not its existence. The consolidated text on the Commission's AI Act Service Desk, as at 27 July 2026, marks all three paragraphs of Article 4 as amended.

VersionWording or effect
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, originalProviders and deployers "shall take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy" of staff and others acting for them
Commission proposal, 19 November 2025The Commission and Member States would "encourage" providers and deployers, removing the direct duty on companies (per William Fry's summary)
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026Providers and deployers "shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy"; no specific level must be guaranteed for any individual

So the proposal to remove the direct duty did not survive. Companies still carry an obligation, but it is judged on the measures taken rather than the level achieved. Bristows describes the result as an obligation "of effort rather than outcome". Amended paragraph 2 commits the Commission and Member States to support providers and deployers, in particular SMEs, including by publishing practical examples. Paragraph 3 asks the AI Board for recommendations.

This is our reading of the published text and guidance. It is not legal advice, and firms with high-risk uses should take their own.

What the Commission expects

The Commission's AI literacy Q&A, updated on 20 October 2026 to reflect the amendment, is the most practical guidance.

  • Who is covered. Staff, and other persons operating or using AI on the organisation's behalf, such as contractors and service providers.
  • No certificate. Organisations can keep an internal record of training and other guidance initiatives instead.
  • No fixed format. The approach depends on context and the risk of the systems in use. Relying only on a vendor's instructions for use is often ineffective, the Q&A says.
  • Suggested minimum content. A general understanding of AI in the organisation, the organisation's role as provider or deployer, the risks of the systems in use, and actions tailored to staff knowledge and context, including legal and ethical aspects.
  • Enforcement. National market surveillance authorities supervise from 2 August 2026 and may impose proportionate penalties.

A proportionate programme for a commercial team

For a 20 to 500 person firm, literacy is easiest to organise by role and by autonomy level. The table is illustrative; adjust it to the tools in your inventory.

RoleWhat they need to knowEvidence to keep
EveryoneApproved tools, the data rule, how to report a mistakePolicy briefing, dated
Sellers and marketersWhere drafting tools err; disclosure rules for chatbots and synthetic mediaShort session per tool
ApproversWhat to check before approving agent output, and when to rejectNamed list, with examples reviewed
Agent and tool ownersAutonomy level, limits, logs, kill switchOwner sign-off on the inventory
Owners of high-risk usesArticle 26 oversight duties, the provider's instructionsTraining record per person

The first row is usually an AI acceptable use policy. The approver row matters most under lowob's rule that nothing sends without a person: an approver who does not know what to check is a signature, not a control.

The lowob view

lowob treats literacy as part of the record, not a training event. The useful evidence is a dated line per person and tool: who was briefed, on what, and who approves their output. It sits beside the AI inventory and the decision log, where a regulator or a customer's security review can read it.

lowob takeaways

  • The duty survived. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 softened Article 4 to "support" but did not remove it from companies.
  • Effort is judged, not level. No individual must reach a set standard; the measures must fit the role and risk.
  • Keep a record. No certificate is needed, but an internal record of who learned what is the natural evidence.
  • Train approvers first. The people who sign off AI output carry the most risk and need the most specific briefing.

Common questions

What does Article 4 of the EU AI Act require?

Since the 2026 amendment, providers and deployers must take measures to support the development of AI literacy among staff and others using AI for them, without guaranteeing a specific level for any individual.

Was the AI literacy obligation removed by the Digital Omnibus?

No. The Commission proposed shifting it to public authorities, but the final text kept a duty on providers and deployers, reframed as supporting AI literacy.

Do employees need an AI literacy certificate?

No. The Commission says no certificate is needed; organisations can keep an internal record of training and guidance.

When is AI literacy enforced?

The duty has applied since 2 February 2025. National market surveillance authorities supervise and enforce it from 2 August 2026.

Sources and notes

  • European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Article 4: AI literacy, consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. Primary legal text; paragraphs marked as amended by the Digital Omnibus.
  • European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Article 3 and Article 26, consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. Primary legal text; definitions and deployer oversight duty.
  • European Commission, AI literacy: questions and answers, updated 20 October 2026. Official guidance, not legally binding; it describes the amendment as entering into force in mid-July 2026.
  • EUR-Lex, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI), 8 July 2026. Primary source for the regulation's date and its entry into force on 27 July 2026.
  • William Fry, EU Digital Omnibus Proposal: Key AI Proposals, December 2025. Law firm briefing on the original proposal, which the final text did not follow on this point.
  • Bristows, The Digital Omnibus on AI: key changes to the EU AI Act, 12 August 2026. Law firm commentary; not legal advice.

Next Move

List every person who approves AI output before it reaches a client, and give each a 30-minute briefing on what to check. Record the date and topic; that is the core of your Article 4 record.
